title: The policy is the business logic

slides.headline: Zoom in and you find the business logic
slides.sub: The first rules for an agent are mechanical. A few layers in, you are writing how the company works.

slides.headline: The first rules are mechanical. Vendors do them well.
slides.sub: Do not send, only draft. Do not delete. Use your own account. The same in every company.

slides.headline: Above the mechanics, every layer is the business
slides.sub: Each layer has its own owner, from IT and security up to the board.

slides.headline: Software used to enforce the rules by omission

right.title: Through an API
points: The agent calls the same endpoint

slides.headline: No vendor can model every customer's business
slides.sub: The mechanical layer is a product. The business layers are the customer's, and the customer has to write them.

slides.label: rules backed by a control
slides.sub: Six more rest on an accepted risk and six on hope. The firm is fictional; the shape is the point.

slides.headline: Where a vendor's control plugs in
items: Send gateway: a new recipient needs a person
Content check: never quote a price
Legal's blocked list: the dispute rule

slides.quote: A skill says how. A policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule, and what stands in the way of breaking it.

slides.headline: Only the business can write its business logic
slides.sub: Write it in layers, each with an owner, and count what is enforced.

image_prompts.prompt: Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait cover slide for a short deck about AI agent rules. At the centre, a large flat magnifying glass hovers over a simple envelope icon representing an email agent. Inside the lens, instead of the envelope's surface, the viewer sees a neat stack of horizontal layers, the lowest ones drawn as small padlocks and toggle switches, the upper ones as tiny icons of an invoice, a handshake and a building. Above the picture, a small uppercase kicker reads 'Agent behaviour policies'. The headline, in a confident serif, reads 'Zoom in and you find the business logic'. Beneath it, a single line of supporting text explains that the first rules for an agent are mechanical, and that a few layers in you are writing how the company works. Generous white space, a thin teal bar along the top edge, no clutter, no people, no logos, no decorative gradients. The mood is calm, precise and editorial, like the cover of a well designed report.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait slide making one statement: the first rules anybody writes for an agent are mechanical, and vendors do them well. Show three simple flat icon tiles in a row, each with a short caption: a paper draft with a pencil labelled 'Do not send, only draft', a bin with a teal line through it labelled 'Do not delete', and a single person badge labelled 'Use your own account'. Beneath the row, a faint repeated pattern of identical small office buildings suggests that these rules are the same in every company. The headline at the top, in a serif typeface, reads 'The first rules are mechanical. Vendors do them well.' Keep the composition sparse and balanced, with plenty of cream space, teal used only for icons and the top bar, and dark grey text. No people, no brand names, no extra statistics, nothing the article does not say.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait diagram showing a behaviour policy as a vertical stack of five labelled layers, drawn top to bottom as rounded white boxes with teal outlines: 'Organisation' at the top with a small building icon, then 'Relationship' with a handshake icon, 'Process' with a flow of three dots, 'Function' with an envelope icon, and 'Mechanics' at the bottom with a padlock and a toggle switch. Short teal arrows between each pair of boxes carry the small italic label 'refines', showing that each layer refines the one beneath it. To the right of each box, a tiny badge names its owner: the board, account managers, finance, HR and legal, the head of operations, and IT and security. The headline above reads 'Above the mechanics, every layer is the business'. A short line at the foot notes that each layer has its own owner. Clear hierarchy, legible labels, generous spacing, no extra layers or numbers.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait comparison slide split into two side by side panels. The left panel, titled 'Through a screen', shows a flat computer window in which an invoice form has a greyed out 'Send' button, with a small note that the button only appears after finance approves; below it, a second window where a payment details panel is hidden behind a role badge. The right panel, tinted pale teal and titled 'Through an API', shows a small robot-like agent icon reaching past the window frame directly to a plug labelled API, calling the same action the button would have called; a dashed outline marks the rule that the screen used to enforce and that is now missing. The headline across the top reads 'Software used to enforce the rules by omission'. Keep each panel to an icon and two short captions, with balanced weight on both sides and no extra text or figures.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait statement slide. The headline in a large serif reads 'No vendor can model every customer's business'. Below it, a simple illustration of a stack of layers cut horizontally: the bottom slab is drawn as a neat, boxed product with a teal ribbon and a small label 'product', identical copies of it lined up to suggest it scales to every customer; the upper slabs are drawn in varied, hand finished shapes, each slightly different, with a small pen beside them labelled 'customer writes'. A short supporting line explains that the mechanical layer is a product, while the business layers belong to the customer, who has to write them. The tone is neutral, not critical of vendors. Plenty of cream space, teal used sparingly, dark grey text, no logos and no numbers.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait statistics slide built around one large figure: '5 of 17' in a big teal serif numeral, with the label 'rules backed by a control' beneath. Under the figure, a row of seventeen small square tiles: five solid teal tiles marked with a small shield for control, six tiles with a teal outline and a small signed paper icon for accepted risk, and six pale grey tiles with a small crossed fingers icon for hope. A short caption says that six more rules rest on an accepted risk and six on hope, and that the firm is fictional while the shape is the point. Clear legend, even spacing, no percentages, no other numbers, and no suggestion that the counts come from a real company.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait list slide titled 'Where a vendor's control plugs in'. Four horizontal cards stacked vertically, each with a teal left edge, a simple flat icon and a short caption. First card: a mail gate icon, 'Send gateway: a new recipient needs a person'. Second card: a magnifier over text with a crossed out price tag, 'Content check: never quote a price'. Third card: a ledger book with a tick, 'Ledger check: invoice approved first'. Fourth card: a list with a stop symbol held by a scales of justice icon, 'Legal's blocked list: the dispute rule'. Each card shows a small plug connecting the product icon to a written rule, suggesting existing products enforcing rules the customer wrote. No brand names, no logos, no numbers, generous spacing, legible type.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A portrait quote slide. A large teal opening quotation mark sits at the upper left. The quotation, set in an italic serif, reads: 'A skill says how. A policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule, and what stands in the way of breaking it.' Beneath the quote, two small flat icons sit side by side as a quiet visual gloss: a sheet labelled 'skill' with a numbered list of steps, and a sheet labelled 'policy layer' with three small markers for allowed, owner and barrier. A small uppercase attribution reads 'From the article'. Abundant cream space, restrained teal, dark grey text, nothing added to the quotation and no other text.

Clean editorial infographic, cream background #faf9f5, teal accents, simple flat icons, no photographs. A closing slide with a solid teal panel filling most of the page and white text. The headline in serif reads 'Only the business can write its business logic'. Beneath it, a short line says to write it in layers, each with an owner, and count what is enforced. A simple white line drawing shows a pen writing on a stack of layered sheets, each sheet carrying a small name tag for its owner, with a little counter beside the stack. At the bottom, in a rounded translucent box, the address sgit.ai/articles/the-behaviour-policy-is-the-business-logic.html is shown for readers who want the full article. Calm, uncluttered, no logos, no numbers beyond the address.
